subject: satnav use and the hippocampus
title: What If You Always Used GPS?

scenes.text: What if you always used GPS? You'd never get lost. Your brain might pay instead.
On every new street, your brain's map centre, the hippocampus, normally lights up as you plan a route.
In a London scan study of twenty-four people, following satnav directions added no extra activity there at all.
London taxi drivers, who memorise the city, have a larger rear hippocampus the longer they've driven.
And in a small three-year study, drivers who leaned on GPS more saw their spatial memory decline faster.
So GPS won't get you lost. It just lets your brain's built-in map quietly switch off.

description:
What if you always used GPS? A 2017 UCL study scanned 24 volunteers navigating a simulation of Soho: their hippocampus spiked on entering new streets, but showed no extra activity when they followed satnav instructions.
London taxi drivers have larger posterior hippocampi that grow with years of driving, and a small 2020 McGill study found more GPS use was linked to steeper spatial memory decline over about three years.
